item.title: Hiroshima Castle: The Rebuilt Carp Castle — Guide
item.description: Hiroshima Castle, nicknamed the Carp Castle, was originally built in the 1590s by the warlord Mori Terumoto as the seat of his domain, a striking black-walled keep on the delta plain. The original survived until 1945, when it was destroyed by the atomic bomb; the present five-storey keep is a faithful concrete reconstruction of 1958, its dark timber-look exterior rising from a broad moat and stone base. Inside is a well-presented museum of the castle’s history and samurai culture, and the top floor gives a view over the rebuilt city.

item.title: Heijo Palace: The Heart of Japan's Ancient Capital — Guide
item.description: Heijo Palace was the political and ceremonial heart of Heijo-kyo, Japan’s capital through most of the 8th-century Nara period, and its vast excavated site — a green plain on the northern edge of the city — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Long left as archaeological fields, it has been brought vividly to life by full-scale reconstructions: the towering vermilion Suzakumon main gate, the majestic Daigokuden (Former Imperial Audience Hall) where the emperor once held state ceremonies, and a garden and excellent museums explaining daily life in the ancient capital.
